title: Metabolism, Metabolic Regulation and Nutritional Requirement of Iron in Aquaculture Species: A Critical Review
content:
Iron homeostasis in aquaculture species involves coordinated systemic and cellular regulation, while deficiency and overload impair physiological functions and may trigger oxidative damage and ferroptosis. This review integrates iron metabolism, dietary requirements, and factors influencing iron bioavailability, providing insights into optimizing iron nutrition and maintaining health in aquaculture species.


ABSTRACT

Iron is an essential cofactor for oxygen transport, electron transfer, DNA synthesis, and Fe-S cluster enzymes, with its redox cycling between Fe2+ and Fe3+, underpinning both its biochemical utility and cytotoxic potential via ROS generation, requiring tight homeostatic regulation across all organisms. In contrast to terrestrial vertebrates, aquatic organisms acquire iron not only from dietary sources but also directly from the surrounding water through the gills. This dual acquisition pathway has driven unique regulatory adaptations of iron homeostasis, maintained through tightly coordinated mechanisms of absorption, transport, and storage. Disruption of these mechanisms, either by deficiency or overload, can impair growth, cause anemia, promote oxidative stress, and aggravate metabolic disorders. This review synthesizes current knowledge of iron uptake routes, systemic regulation, storage, and recycling in major aquaculture species. In addition, it provides an overview of dietary iron requirements, iron deficiency and overload, and the effects of feed composition, mineral sources, functional additives and environmental factors on iron bioavailability. Finally, the review discusses ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of programmed cell death associated with lipid peroxidation, and highlights critical knowledge gaps and research priorities for improving iron nutrition and metabolic health in aquaculture species.
